n31561.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
The composition $R_d(\alpha)R_{d'}(\beta)$ is a rotation, i.e.\ conjugate
to some $R_z(\gamma)$ by an isometry, which gives
$\|R_d(\alpha)R_{d'}(\beta)-\id\|^2 = 2(1-\cos\gamma)
= 3 - \tr(R_d(\alpha)R_{d'}(\beta))
= 3 - (\cos\alpha + \cos\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta)$.
Writing the right hand side as
$2(1-\cos\alpha) + 2(1-\cos\beta) - (1-\cos\alpha)(1-\cos\beta)$
and using $2(1-\cos x) \leq x^2$ (with equality only at $x = 0$)
yields the bound and the equality condition.
This is a direct route to \cite{polyhedron.without.rupert}, Lemma 12,
that avoids the Jensen-inequality argument of Lemma 11 and the
doubling induction.
\end{proof}

n31569.content:
\begin{proof}
\uses{lem:RxRy}
\leanok
Write $R_z$ and $R_y$ for rotations about the third and second axes.
After dropping the norm-one projection and canceling the common rotations,
it suffices to bound
\[
  \|R_z(\alpha-\overline{\alpha})R_y(\phi)
       -R_y(\overline{\varphi})R_z(\theta-\overline{\theta})\|.
\]
Insert $R_y(\Phi)$ with the ordinary midpoint $\Phi=(\phi+\overline{\varphi})/2$.
On each side, the two angle changes are bounded by $\varepsilon$ and
$\varepsilon/2$. Lemma~\ref{lem:RxRy}, applied after canceling the common
rotations, bounds each difference strictly by
$\sqrt{\varepsilon^2+(\varepsilon/2)^2}=\sqrt{5}\varepsilon/2$.
If both angle changes vanish, strictness follows from $\varepsilon>0$;
otherwise it follows from the equality condition in that lemma.
The triangle inequality gives the result. The weighted intermediate angle
used in \cite{polyhedron.without.rupert}, Lemma 16, is not needed for this
uniform bound.
\end{proof}

n31570.title: Rupert Polyhedron iff Rupert Set

n31577.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
This is a mild generalization of \cite{polyhedron.without.rupert}, Lemma 18.

Since $S \in \hull V$, we have
\[ S = \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j V_j \]
for some $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m \in [0,1]$ with
\[ 1 = \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j  \]
Therefore
\[
\langle S ,w \rangle = \left\langle  \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j V_j ,w \right\rangle
=  \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j \left\langle   V_j ,w \right\rangle
\le   \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j \max_{i} \langle V_i ,w\rangle
\]
\[
=  \max_{i} \langle V_i ,w\rangle \sum_{j=1}^m \lambda_j
=  \max_{i} \langle V_i ,w\rangle
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

n31578.content:
\begin{lemma} \label{lem:leq1}
\lean{GlobalTheorem.rotation_third_partials_bounded}
\leanok
    Let $S \in \R^3$, let $w \in \R^2$ be a unit vector, and set $f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = \langle R(x_3) M(x_1,x_2)S,w \rangle$. Then for all $x_1,x_2,x_3 \in \R$ and any $i,j,k \in \{1,2,3\}$ it holds that
    \[
        \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 f}{\mathrm{d}x_i \mathrm{d}x_j}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\right|\leq \|S\|
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}^3 f}{\mathrm{d}x_i \mathrm{d}x_j \mathrm{d}x_k}(x_1,x_2,x_3)\right|\leq \|S\|.
    \]
    (\cite{polyhedron.without.rupert} normalizes $f$ by $1/\|S\|$ and bounds the
    partials by $1$; we keep $f$ unnormalized and carry the $\|S\|$ instead,
    which composes with the remainder bound of \cref{lem:n2} at $M = \|S\| \leq 1$.)
\end{lemma}

n31579.content:
\begin{proof}\leanok
The second-partial bound is \cite{polyhedron.without.rupert}, Lemma 19.  For
the third partials (and, in the formalization, every higher order at once) we
argue by closure instead of enumeration: the family of functions
$\pm \langle (\pm R/R')(\alpha)\, (\partial_\theta^a \partial_\phi^b
M)(\theta,\phi)\, S, w\rangle$ with $a, b \le 2$ is closed under all three
partial derivatives --- an $\alpha$-derivative steps the head around its
four-cycle $R \to R' \to -R \to -R'$, and a $\theta$- or $\phi$-derivative
bumps one grid index, folding back with a sign at the edge since
$\partial_\theta^3 = -\partial_\theta$ and
$\partial_\phi^3 = -\partial_\phi$.  Every member is bounded by $\|S\|$
because each factor has operator norm at most one, so iterating the closure
bounds all iterated partials.
\end{proof}

n31580.content:
\begin{lemma} \label{lem:n2}
\lean{GlobalTheorem.bounded_partials_control_difference2}
\leanok
    Let $f:\R^n\to \R$ be a $C^3$-function, let
    $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n \geq 0$, and let
    $x_1,\dots,x_n,y_1,\dots,y_n \in \R$ be such that
    $|x_i-y_i|\leq \varepsilon_i$ for all $i$.
    If, for some $M \in \R$,
    \(
        \left|\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k}f(v)\right| \leq M
    \)
    for all $i,j,k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ and all $v \in \R^n$, then
    \[
    |f(x)-f(y)|\leq \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i |\partial_{x_i} f(x)|
      + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j
          |\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_j} f(x)|
      + \frac{M}{6}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i\Big)^3.
    \]
    (At $M = 1$ and $\varepsilon_1 = \dots = \varepsilon_n = \varepsilon$ this
    recovers the isotropic remainder $\frac{n^3}{6}\varepsilon^3$.)
\end{lemma}

n31581.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
This strengthens \cite{polyhedron.without.rupert}, Lemma 20, by one Taylor
order and per-axis radii: expand $g(t) = f((1-t)x + ty)$ to second order with
Lagrange remainder, bound $|g'(0)|$ by the first sum, $|g''(0)|/2$ by the
second (the second partials are evaluated exactly at $x$, not bounded), and
$|g'''(c)| \le M (\sum_i \varepsilon_i)^3$ using the third-partial bound.
\end{proof}

n31584.title: Global Theorem
n31584.content:
\begin{theorem}[Global Theorem] \label{thm:global}
\lean{GlobalTheorem.global_theorem}
\leanok
    Let $\PPP$ be a pointsymmetric convex polyhedron with radius $\rho =1$ and let $S \in \PPP$. Further let $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha}\in \R$, let
    $\epsilon_\alpha, \epsilon_{\theta_1}, \epsilon_{\phi_1}, \epsilon_{\theta_2}, \epsilon_{\phi_2} \geq 0$
    be per-axis radii, and let $w\in\R^2$ be a unit vector. Denote $\overline{M_1}\coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$, $ \overline{M_2}\coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2)$ as well as $\overline{M_1}^{\theta} \coloneqq M^\theta(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$, $\overline{M_1}^{\phi} \coloneqq M^\phi(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$ and analogously for $\overline{M_2}^{\theta}, \overline{M_2}^{\phi}$. Finally set
    \begin{align*}
        G \coloneqq{}& \langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}S,w \rangle - \epsilon_\alpha|\langle R'(\overline{\alpha})  \overline{M_1}S,w \rangle| - \epsilon_{\theta_1}|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\theta S,w \rangle| - \epsilon_{\phi_1}|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\phi S,w \rangle|\\
        &- \frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon_\alpha^2|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}S,w \rangle|
          + 2\epsilon_\alpha\epsilon_{\theta_1}|\langle R'(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\theta S,w \rangle| + 2\epsilon_\alpha\epsilon_{\phi_1}|\langle R'(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\phi S,w \rangle|\\
        &\qquad\quad + \epsilon_{\theta_1}^2|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^{\theta\theta} S,w \rangle| + 2\epsilon_{\theta_1}\epsilon_{\phi_1}|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^{\theta\phi} S,w \rangle| + \epsilon_{\phi_1}^2|\langle R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^{\phi\phi} S,w \rangle|\big)\\
        &- \frac{(\epsilon_\alpha+\epsilon_{\theta_1}+\epsilon_{\phi_1})^3}{6},\\
        H_P \coloneqq{}& \langle \overline{M_2}P,w \rangle + \epsilon_{\theta_2}|\langle \overline{M_2}^\theta P,w \rangle|+\epsilon_{\phi_2}|\langle  \overline{M_2}^\varphi P,w \rangle|\\
        &+ \frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon_{\theta_2}^2|\langle \overline{M_2}^{\theta\theta} P,w \rangle| + 2\epsilon_{\theta_2}\epsilon_{\phi_2}|\langle \overline{M_2}^{\theta\phi} P,w \rangle| + \epsilon_{\phi_2}^2|\langle \overline{M_2}^{\phi\phi} P,w \rangle|\big) + \frac{(\epsilon_{\theta_2}+\epsilon_{\phi_2})^3}{6}, \quad \text{ for } P \in \PPP.
    \end{align*}
    If $G>\max_{P\in \PPP} H_P$ then there does not exist a solution to Rupert's condition with
    $$(\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in U \coloneqq [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\epsilon_{\theta_1}]\times[\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\epsilon_{\phi_1}]\times[\overline{\theta}_2\pm\epsilon_{\theta_2}]\times[\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\epsilon_{\phi_2}]\times[\overline{\alpha}\pm\epsilon_\alpha] \subseteq \R^5.$$

    (This is a second-order, anisotropic strengthening of
    \cite{polyhedron.without.rupert}, Theorem 17, whose penalty is first-order
    and isotropic with quadratic remainders $9\epsilon^2/2$ and $2\epsilon^2$:
    here the exact second partials at the center pose are charged with
    per-axis weights — with multiplicities from the symmetric Hessian table —
    and only the cubic Lagrange remainders
    $(\epsilon_\alpha+\epsilon_{\theta_1}+\epsilon_{\phi_1})^3/6$ and
    $(\epsilon_{\theta_2}+\epsilon_{\phi_2})^3/6$ are bounded via
    Lemma~\ref{lem:leq1}. On the diagonal
    $\epsilon_\alpha = \epsilon_{\theta_1} = \dots = \epsilon$, these are
    $\frac{3^3}{6}\epsilon^3 = \frac{9\epsilon^3}{2}$ and
    $\frac{2^3}{6}\epsilon^3 = \frac{4\epsilon^3}{3}$.)
\end{theorem}

Define $M = M(\theta, \phi)$ and $\overline{M} = M(\overline{\theta}, \overline{\varphi})$ and let $P, Q \in \R^3$ with $\|P\|, \|Q\| \leq 1$. Assume that

  Then:

        \frac{\langle \overline{M} P,\overline{M} (P-Q)\rangle - 2 \epsilon \|P-Q\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M} P\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M}(P-Q)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)}.
    \]
\end{lemma}

n31608.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
An isometry preserves inner products, so congruence implies equality of the Gram matrices.
Conversely, since the $Q_i$ form a basis, define a linear map $L$ by $L(Q_i)=P_i$.
The equality $P^t P = Q^t Q$ says that
$\langle L(Q_i),L(Q_j)\rangle=\langle Q_i,Q_j\rangle$ for every $i,j$.
Expanding arbitrary vectors in this basis shows that $L$ preserves all inner products,
and hence is the required linear isometry.

    If $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent then $\langle P_i,P_j\rangle = \langle LQ_i,LQ_j\rangle = \langle Q_i,Q_j\rangle$, thus $P^t P = Q^t Q$.
    For the other direction, we claim that $L \coloneqq PQ^{-1}$ is orthonormal and satisfies that $P_i = LQ_i$ for all $i=1,2,3$.
    Indeed,  $L^t L = (PQ^{-1})^t (PQ^{-1}) = (Q^t)^{-1} P^t P Q^{-1} = \mathrm{Id}$ and it holds that $LQ=PQ^{-1}Q=P$, thus $LQ_i = P_i$.
\end{proof}

n31609.title: Local Theorem
n31609.content:
\begin{theorem}[Local Theorem] \label{thm:local}
\leanok
\lean{Local.local_theorem}
    Let $\PPP$ be a polyhedron with radius $\rho=1$ and $P_1, P_2, P_3, Q_1, Q_2, Q_3 \in \PPP$ be not necessarily distinct. Assume that $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent.

    Let $\epsilon>0$ and $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha}\in \R$, then set $\overline{X_1}\coloneqq X(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1), \overline{X_2}\coloneqq X(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$ as well as $\overline{M_1}\coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1), \overline{M_2}\coloneqq M(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$.
    Assume that there exist $\sigma_P, \sigma_Q \in \{0,1\}$ such that
    \[
        (-1)^{\sigma_P} \langle \overline{X_1},P_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon \quad \text{and} \quad
        (-1)^{\sigma_Q} \langle \overline{X_2}, Q_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon, \tag{A$_\epsilon$}
    \]
    for all $i=1,2,3$.
    Moreover, assume that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are $\epsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1)$ and that $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ are $\epsilon$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$.
    Finally, assume that for all $i = 1,2,3$ and any $Q_j \in \PPP \setminus Q_i$ it holds~that
    \[
        \frac{\langle \overline{M_2}Q_i,\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\rangle - 2 \epsilon \|Q_i-Q_j\| \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2}Q_i\|+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(Q_i-Q_j)\|+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon\big)} > \frac{\sqrt{5} \epsilon + \delta}{r}, \tag{B$_\epsilon$}
    \]
    for some $r >0$ such that $\min_{i=1,2,3}\| \overline{M_2}Q_i \| > r + \sqrt{2} \epsilon$ and for some $\delta \in \R$ with
    \[
        \delta \geq \max_{i=1,2,3}\left\|R(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}P_i - \overline{M_2}Q_i\right\|/2.
    \]
    Then there exists no solution to Rupert's problem $R(\alpha) M(\theta_1,\phi_1)\PPP \subset  M(\theta_2,\phi_2)\PPP^\circ$ with
    \[
        (\theta_1, \phi_1, \theta_2, \phi_2, \alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\epsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\epsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\epsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\epsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\epsilon] \coloneqq U \subseteq \R^5.
    \]
\end{theorem}

n31626.content:
\begin{theorem}[Rational Global Theorem] \label{thm:global_rational}
\leanok
\lean{RationalApprox.GlobalTheorem.rational_global}
    Let $\PPP$ be a pointsymmetric convex polyhedron with radius $\rho =1$ and $\widetilde{\PPP}$ a $\kappa$-rational approximation. Let $\widetilde{S} \in \widetilde{\PPP}$. Further let
    $\epsilon_\alpha, \epsilon_{\theta_1}, \epsilon_{\phi_1}, \epsilon_{\theta_2}, \epsilon_{\phi_2} \in \Q_{\geq 0}$
    be per-axis radii and $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha}\in \Q \cap [-4,4]$.
    Let $w\in\Q^2$ be a unit vector. Denote $\overline{M_1}\coloneqq M_{\Q}(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$, $ \overline{M_2}\coloneqq M_{\Q}(\overline{\theta}_2, \overline{\varphi}_2)$ as well as $\overline{M_1}^{\theta} \coloneqq M_{\Q}^\theta(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$, $\overline{M_1}^{\phi} \coloneqq M_{\Q}^\phi(\overline{\theta}_1, \overline{\varphi}_1)$ and analogously for $\overline{M_2}^{\theta}, \overline{M_2}^{\phi}$. Write
    $E_1 \coloneqq \epsilon_\alpha + \epsilon_{\theta_1} + \epsilon_{\phi_1}$ and
    $E_2 \coloneqq \epsilon_{\theta_2} + \epsilon_{\phi_2}$, and set
    \begin{align*}
        G^{\Q} \coloneqq{}& \langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}\widetilde{S},w \rangle - \epsilon_\alpha|\langle R_{\Q}'(\overline{\alpha})  \overline{M_1}\widetilde{S},w \rangle| - \epsilon_{\theta_1}|\langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\theta \widetilde{S},w \rangle| - \epsilon_{\phi_1}|\langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\phi \widetilde{S},w \rangle| \\
        &- \frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon_\alpha^2|\langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}\widetilde{S},w \rangle|
          + 2\epsilon_\alpha\epsilon_{\theta_1}|\langle R_{\Q}'(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\theta \widetilde{S},w \rangle| + 2\epsilon_\alpha\epsilon_{\phi_1}|\langle R_{\Q}'(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^\phi \widetilde{S},w \rangle|\\
        &\qquad\quad + \epsilon_{\theta_1}^2|\langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^{\theta\theta} \widetilde{S},w \rangle| + 2\epsilon_{\theta_1}\epsilon_{\phi_1}|\langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^{\theta\phi} \widetilde{S},w \rangle| + \epsilon_{\phi_1}^2|\langle R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}^{\phi\phi} \widetilde{S},w \rangle|\big)\\
        & \hspace{9cm}- \frac{E_1^3}{6} - 4\kappa \big( 1 + E_1 + \tfrac12 E_1^2\big),\\
        H^{\Q}_P \coloneqq{}& \langle \overline{M_2}P,w \rangle + \epsilon_{\theta_2}|\langle \overline{M_2}^\theta P,w \rangle|+\epsilon_{\phi_2}|\langle  \overline{M_2}^\varphi P,w \rangle|\\
        &+ \frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon_{\theta_2}^2|\langle \overline{M_2}^{\theta\theta} P,w \rangle| + 2\epsilon_{\theta_2}\epsilon_{\phi_2}|\langle \overline{M_2}^{\theta\phi} P,w \rangle| + \epsilon_{\phi_2}^2|\langle \overline{M_2}^{\phi\phi} P,w \rangle|\big) + \frac{E_2^3}{6} + 3\kappa\big( 1+E_2+\tfrac12 E_2^2\big).
    \end{align*}
    If $G^{\Q}>\max_{P\in \widetilde{\PPP}} H^{\Q}_P$ then there does not exist a solution to Rupert's condition to $\PPP$ with
    \[
    (\theta_1,\varphi_1,\theta_2,\varphi_2,\alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\epsilon_{\theta_1}]\times[\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\epsilon_{\phi_1}]\times[\overline{\theta}_2\pm\epsilon_{\theta_2}]\times[\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\epsilon_{\phi_2}]\times[\overline{\alpha}\pm\epsilon_\alpha].
    \]
    (On the diagonal $\epsilon_\alpha = \dots = \epsilon$ the slack terms are
    $4\kappa(1+3\epsilon+\tfrac92\epsilon^2)$ and
    $3\kappa(1+2\epsilon+2\epsilon^2)$.)
\end{theorem}

n31635.title: Rational Local Theorem
n31635.content:
\begin{theorem}[Rational Local Theorem]
\label{thm:local_rational}
\leanok
\lean{RationalApprox.LocalTheorem.rational_local}
\uses{def:ekspanning}
    Let $\PPP$ be a polyhedron with radius $\rho=1$ and $\widetilde{P}_i$ be a $\kappa$-rational approximation of $P_i \in \PPP$. Set $\widetilde{\PPP} = \{\widetilde{P}_i \text{ for } P_i \in \PPP \}$. Let $P_1, P_2, P_3, Q_1, Q_2, Q_3 \in \PPP$ be not necessarily distinct and assume that $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$ are congruent.
    Let $\epsilon>0$ and $\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1,\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2,\overline{\alpha}\in \Q \cap [-4,4]$.
    Set $\overline{X_1}\coloneqq X_{\Q}(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1), \overline{X_2}\coloneqq X_{\Q}(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$ as well as $\overline{M_1}\coloneqq M_{\Q}(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1), \overline{M_2}\coloneqq M_{\Q}(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$.
    Assume that there exist $\sigma_P, \sigma_Q \in \{0,1\}$ such that
    \[
        (-1)^{\sigma_P} \langle \overline{X_1},\widetilde{P}_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon + 3\kappa \quad \text{and} \quad
        (-1)^{\sigma_Q} \langle \overline{X_2}, \widetilde{Q}_i\rangle>\sqrt{2}\varepsilon + 3\kappa, \tag{A$^{\Q}_\epsilon$}
    \]
    for all $i=1,2,3$.
    Moreover, assume that $\widetilde{P}_1,\widetilde{P}_2,\widetilde{P}_3$ are $\epsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_1,\overline{\varphi}_1)$ and that $\widetilde{Q}_1,\widetilde{Q}_2,\widetilde{Q}_3$ are $\epsilon$-$\kappa$-spanning for $(\overline{\theta}_2,\overline{\varphi}_2)$. Let $\sqrt[+]{x}$ and $\sqrt[-]{x}$ be upper- and lower-square-root functions (bounding $\sqrt{x}$ from above/below for all real $x \geq 0$, with rational output on rational input), then set $\|Z\|_{+} \coloneqq \sqrt[+]{\|Z\|^2}$ and $\|Z\|_{-} \coloneqq \sqrt[-]{\|Z\|^2}$ for $Z \in \R^n$.
    Finally, assume that for all $i = 1,2,3$ and any $\widetilde{Q}_j \in \widetilde{\PPP} \setminus \widetilde{Q}_i$ it holds that
    \[
        \frac{\langle \overline{M_2}\widetilde{Q}_i,\overline{M_2}(\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j)\rangle - 10\kappa - 2 \epsilon ( \|\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j\|_{+} + 2 \kappa ) \cdot  (\sqrt{2}+\varepsilon)}{ \big(\|\overline{M_2}\widetilde{Q}_i\|_{+}+\sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 3\kappa \big) \cdot \big(\|\overline{M_2}(\widetilde{Q}_i-\widetilde{Q}_j)\|_{+}+2 \sqrt{2} \varepsilon + 6\kappa\big)} > \frac{\sqrt{5} \epsilon + \delta}{r}, \tag{B$^{\Q}_\epsilon$}
    \]
    for some $r >0$ such that $\min_{i=1,2,3}\| \overline{M_2}\widetilde{Q}_i \|_{-} > r + \sqrt{2} \epsilon + 3\kappa$ and for some $\delta \in \R$ with
    \[
        \delta \geq \max_{i=1,2,3}\left\|R_{\Q}(\overline{\alpha}) \overline{M_1}\widetilde{P}_i-\overline{M_2}\widetilde{Q}_i\right\|_{+}/2 + 3\kappa.
    \]
    Then there exists no solution to Rupert's problem $R(\alpha) M(\theta_1,\phi_1)\PPP \subset  M(\theta_2,\phi_2)\PPP^\circ$ with
    \[
        (\theta_1, \phi_1, \theta_2, \phi_2, \alpha) \in [\overline{\theta}_1\pm\epsilon,\overline{\varphi}_1\pm\epsilon,\overline{\theta}_2\pm\epsilon,\overline{\varphi}_2\pm\epsilon,\overline{\alpha}\pm\epsilon] \subseteq \R^5.
    \]

    (In the Lean formalization, the applied vector $\overline{M_2}\widetilde{Q}_i$ in the
    $r$-condition $\| \overline{M_2}\widetilde{Q}_i \|_{-} > r + \sqrt{2} \epsilon + 3\kappa$
    is additionally rounded down componentwise to a multiple of $10^{-13}$ ---
    \texttt{Pose.rotM₂Rℚ}, as in condition B$^{\Q}_\epsilon$ --- so that the
    checker's lower norm runs on small denominators; the resulting perturbation of
    at most $2 \cdot 10^{-13}$ is absorbed into the $3\kappa$ term.)
\end{theorem}
